topic_title: Basic economic problem: scarcity and exercise of choice
topic: 1.1 Basic economic problem: scarcity and exercise of choice
qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.canonical_answer: Resources are limited relative to the wants that could be satisfied with them.
marking_guidance: Meaning/definition and essential element (1): the relationship between limited resources and competing wants; credit the complete meaning.
objective_titles: Describe the nature of the economic problem (limited resources and unlimited wants)

items.prompt: Identify two features that together create the basic economic problem.
items.canonical_answer: Available resources are limited; wants competing for their use exceed what they can satisfy.
marking_guidance: Characteristic (1): limited resources. Distinction/example of the second feature (1): competing wants exceed what those resources can satisfy.
objective_titles: Describe the nature of the economic problem (limited resources and unlimited wants)

items.prompt: Explain why unsold bicycle tyres at an invented Tsumeb repair workshop do not establish that the economy has no scarcity.
items.canonical_answer: Unsold tyres show that those particular products have not all been bought. They do not show unlimited resources: mechanics’ time, materials and space still have competing uses.
marking_guidance: Confusion/boundary (1): unsold finished products do not imply unlimited productive resources. Test to distinguish (1): check whether resources still have competing feasible uses.
objective_titles: Describe the nature of the economic problem (limited resources and unlimited wants)

items.prompt: Explain the difference between opportunity cost and the combined value of every rejected option.
items.canonical_answer: Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone. Combining all rejected options counts alternatives that may not have been available together.
marking_guidance: Difference (1): next-best feasible alternative rather than all alternatives. Contrast/test (1): mutually exclusive alternatives cannot all have been chosen instead.

items.prompt: Explain the opportunity cost when a learner chooses an hour of revision instead of a walk with friends. The walk is the next-best feasible use of that hour.
items.canonical_answer: The opportunity cost is the enjoyment or companionship forgone from the walk, because it is the next-best feasible alternative ruled out by revision.
marking_guidance: Context (1): benefit of the specified walk forgone. Reason/conclusion (1): it is the next-best feasible alternative excluded by the revision choice.

items.prompt: Explain opportunity cost using a production possibility frontier for an invented Namibian workshop. Weekly feasible combinations (bicycle services, handcart services) are (0,8), (2,6), (4,4), (6,2), (8,0). Resources and technology are fixed and each combination uses them efficiently. Plot bicycles horizontally and handcarts vertically. Explain moving from (4,4) to (6,2).
items.canonical_answer: Label both axes in services per week and join the five combinations with a straight frontier. Moving from (4,4) to (6,2) gains two bicycle services and sacrifices two handcart services. The opportunity cost is one handcart service per extra bicycle service. This is movement along the existing frontier, not increased productive capacity.
marking_guidance: Axes/labels (1): bicycle and handcart services per week. Initial position/original curve (2): correct five combinations (1), straight frontier through them (1). Change/control (1): (4,4) to (6,2) with unchanged resources. Explanation (2): two handcart services sacrificed (1) to gain two bicycle services (1). Interpretation (1): one handcart service per extra bicycle service. Total 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate the hub’s choice of tutoring. Invented teaching situation: Sand River Youth Hub in Rundu can staff one afternoon activity, mathematics tutoring or bicycle-maintenance training. Both have applicants. Its N$800 materials budget is sufficient for either activity, but staffing limits it to one. It prioritises urgent mathematics support and ranks tutoring first, bicycle training second.
items.canonical_answer: Tutoring addresses the stated urgent priority and therefore puts the scarce staffed session to its preferred use. However, applicants lose the valuable bicycle-training opportunity. Tutoring is justified if the urgency of mathematics support outweighs that sacrifice under the hub’s objective. A new volunteer and time slot could change feasibility, so the judgement should be revisited if the training could then run without displacing another valued use.
marking_guidance: Argument for (2): meets mathematics priority (1), using the scarce staffed session to address urgent need (1). Argument against (2): training benefit forgone (1), reducing opportunities for its applicants (1). Condition/trade-off (1): relative urgency under the stated objective. Judgement (2): choose tutoring on that priority (1), reconsider if the constraint changes and both become feasible (1). Total 7.

items.prompt: Define scarcity (2). Identify one scarce resource in a repair workshop and one feasible alternative use (2). Explain opportunity cost (2). Identify the non-monetary benefit forgone when a learner chooses revision over a walk, with the walk stated to be the next-best feasible activity (2).
items.canonical_answer: Scarcity means limited resources relative to competing wants. Mechanics’ time can service bicycles or handcarts. Opportunity cost is the value of the next-best feasible alternative forgone. The learner sacrifices the enjoyment or companionship of the walk, which the stated ranking makes the relevant alternative.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): limited resources (1), relative to competing wants (1). Identification, separate points (2): mechanics’ time (1), handcart servicing as an alternative to bicycle servicing (1). Explanation (2): next-best feasible alternative (1), its value forgone (1). Final identification (2): enjoyment/companionship of the walk (1), tied to the supplied next-best activity (1). Marks allocation totals 8.
objective_titles: Describe the nature of the economic problem (limited resources and unlimited wants)

items.prompt: Invented teaching situation: Sand River Youth Hub in Rundu can staff one afternoon activity, mathematics tutoring or bicycle-maintenance training. Both have applicants. Its N$800 materials budget is sufficient for either activity, but staffing limits it to one. It prioritises urgent mathematics support and ranks tutoring first, bicycle training second. Describe the resource constraint, choice and opportunity cost (6). Explain why the next-best feasible activity, rather than every possible activity added together, supplies the opportunity cost (7). Discuss the decision if an additional volunteer and a second afternoon become available for training without reducing tutoring, while other demands on these resources must still be checked (7).
items.canonical_answer: The staffed afternoon is limited, both activities are wanted, and the hub selects tutoring. Bicycle training is feasible and ranks next, so its benefit is forgone. The same staffed session cannot support both activities. Selecting tutoring excludes training then; the stated ranking establishes training as the best alternative. Adding other possible activities would aggregate mutually exclusive uses rather than identify what could replace tutoring. Tutoring remains valuable under the urgent-support priority. Training also benefits applicants, so the extra volunteer and afternoon could make both activities preferable to choosing only one. That judgement depends on confirming that the additional time, room and materials do not displace another more valued use.
marking_guidance: Context/data description (6): scarce staffed afternoon (1), two wanted activities (1), tutoring chosen (1), training feasible (1), training next-ranked (1), training benefit forgone (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): shared staff/time cannot support both (1); selection excludes training then (1); training could replace tutoring (1); ranking makes it best alternative (1); opportunity cost values its benefit (1); other activities may be mutually exclusive (1); aggregating them misstates the feasible sacrifice (1). Both sides and judgement (7): tutoring serves priority (1), urgent need supports it (1); training has benefits (1), applicants gain if it runs (1); new resources change feasibility (1); prefer both if other uses are not displaced (1); check that condition before concluding (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Evaluate two decisions in separate response plans, seven marks each. Invented teaching situation: Sand River Youth Hub in Rundu can staff one afternoon activity, mathematics tutoring or bicycle-maintenance training. Both have applicants. Its N$800 materials budget is sufficient for either activity, but staffing limits it to one. It prioritises urgent mathematics support and ranks tutoring first, bicycle training second. Case 1 uses the original one-session constraint. Case 2 adds a volunteer and a second afternoon for training without reducing tutoring, but the hub must check other demands on these resources. Plan an argument for, an argument against, a decisive condition and a judgement for each case.
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: tutoring serves urgent mathematics needs; training benefits are sacrificed. Relative urgency under the stated objective decides whether tutoring is justified. Choose tutoring if that priority outweighs the training sacrifice. Case 2: providing both activities can retain both benefits with the additional volunteer and afternoon. Other demands on the new resources remain a possible sacrifice. Support the revised combination only if those uses do not displace something more valuable under the hub’s objective.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for meets priority (1) and urgent need (1); argument against loses training (1) and applicants’ skill benefits (1); condition is relative urgency (1); judgement chooses tutoring (1) because that condition matches the objective (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument for retains tutoring (1) and adds training (1); argument against uses volunteer time (1) and another room/time opportunity (1); condition is no displacement of a more valued use (1); judgement favours both (1) only after checking that condition (1). Total 14; each plan totals 7.
